literal: Various tomb epitaphs, the Pingdeng Temple entry in Record of Buddhist Monasteries of Luoyang juan 2, and the colophon to the Fanyang Wang stele in Record of Metal and Stone juan 21 prove that the biography's Wenmu is an error for Wumu.
idiomatic: Epitaphs, Luoyang's monastic record (Pingdeng Temple, juan 2), and Zhao Mingcheng's stele note (Record of Metal and Stone, juan 21, Fanyang Wang) show the life should read Wumu, not Wenmu.

literal: Kept constantly at his side; at four years the Empress Dowager personally gave him the name Xun, style Yuandao; thereupon a great amnesty. Imperial Overview juan 148
idiomatic: "Kept at his side; at four the Empress Dowager named him Xun, styled Yuandao; a great amnesty followed"—Imperial Overview, juan 148

literal: 〈page 723〉
idiomatic: folio 723

literal: Below "kept constantly at his side" it reads: "Edict: 'Of old, at Mount Tu there was Yu, whose fair name stands in the Xia canon;
idiomatic: After "kept at his side" the text has: "Edict: 'In antiquity Yu of Mount Tu bore a name honored in the Xia canon;

literal: Ren and Si were made consorts, and Changfa shone forth in the Zhou documents.
idiomatic: Ren and Si were paired, and Changfa blazed in the Zhou records.

literal: Thus they could gather brightness to the great succession and extend the throne eight hundred years.
idiomatic: So they gathered glory for the great line and stretched the throne eight hundred years.

literal: Since the eldest son was born, it is now four years, yet his name is not trusted in the four quarters and his abundant merit is not displayed in the court sleeves—this is not how to take the distant plan as law and fully illumine ritual measure.
idiomatic: Four years since the heir was born, yet his name is unknown abroad and his merit unseen at court—not the way to honor distant design and brighten ritual order.

literal: The Empress Dowager personally issued a bright decree and gave him a name; according with virtue and matching righteousness, his name is Xun and his style Yuandao.
idiomatic: The Empress Dowager herself proclaimed his name in accord with virtue and rite: Xun, styled Yuandao.

literal: The state's fortune is forever lofty; the heir has a resting-place; the omen of the endless begins here.
idiomatic: The realm's fortune stands firm; the heir is secured; endless blessing begins here.

literal: '" Thereupon a great amnesty throughout the realm.
idiomatic: '" Then came amnesty for all under heaven.

literal: This is the original text of the Book of Wei biography of Yuan Xun.
idiomatic: That is the Book of Wei's full wording in the biography of Yuan Xun.

literal: From "at four years" to "thereupon a great amnesty" in this biography is an abbreviation by the Northern History based on this passage.
idiomatic: Northern History compresses this passage into the span from "at four years" to "great amnesty."

literal: Today you personally see me. Comprehensive Records juan 84b, Biographies of Xiaowen's Six Princes, has "jin" (today) as "ru" (as if)—suspected error.
idiomatic: "Today you see me in person": Comprehensive Records 84b (Six Princes of Xiaowen) reads jin (today) as ru (as if)—likely corrupt.

literal: Seeking attendance on important matters by reason of office. Comprehensive Records juan 84b reads "Seeking attendance though office is not intimate and important"—suspected error.
idiomatic: "Seeking key posts by office": Comprehensive Records 84b has "though the post is neither close nor vital"—probably wrong.

literal: The five benefits, by luck ending, met with conspicuous punishment. Palace Edition textual notes state: "Zai Yi's memorial of remonstrance ends at this sentence; the text is still unfinished—it must be deficient.
idiomatic: "Five gains that cheat fate end in public execution": Palace Edition textual notes say Yuan Yi's remonstrance stops here mid-sentence—the passage is incomplete.

literal: Comprehensive Records juan 84b after this sentence has: "This affair may serve as the utmost mirror; the Empress Dowager deeply accepted it.
idiomatic: Comprehensive Records 84b adds after this line: "Let this be the sternest warning; the Empress Dowager took it deeply to heart."

literal: Commentary: The memorial text is unfinished and does not propose how to handle the matter—what does "deeply accepted" refer to?
idiomatic: Note: the memorial breaks off without a remedy—what could "deeply accepted" mean?

literal: It is known that Comprehensive Records only supplied two sentences by conjecture and they are not original text.
idiomatic: Those two lines in Comprehensive Records are editorial guesswork, not source text.

literal: Prime Tortoise juan 288
idiomatic: Prime Tortoise, juan 288

literal: 〈page 3396〉
idiomatic: folio 3396

literal: "Five benefits, luck" reads "the five benefits' deceit," and this sentence together with the preceding "Xinyuan
idiomatic: Prime Tortoise reads "five benefits' fraud" for "five benefits, luck," and joins this line with the earlier "Xinyuan

literal: 〈adding the particle zhi〉
idiomatic: (with the particle zhi added)

literal: traitors do not ascend the Bright Hall" and moved it to the head of the memorial—the sense is somewhat smoother; this too is because the memorial text is incomplete and was altered in intent, and is also not original text.
idiomatic: traitors shall not enter the Bright Hall," shifting both to the memorial's opening for smoother sense—another repair where the text was broken, not the original.

literal: This biography ultimately derives from the Northern History; how the Northern History lost text below this point can no longer be known.
idiomatic: The life ultimately comes from Northern History; what it omitted below is beyond recovery.

literal: Examination finds Tongdian juan 16 has the following text: In the time of Emperor Xiaoming, Prince of Qinghe Yi, because official personnel were out of order, submitted a memorial saying: "Emperor Xiaowen regulated that men who entered office by birth should, by the constant of noble and base in their clans, have fixed standing.
idiomatic: Tongdian juan 16 preserves this: Under Xiaoming, Prince of Qinghe Yi, finding official ranks disordered, memorialized: "Xiaowen decreed that entrants by birth should rank by hereditary grade with fixed standing.

literal: If according with salary and shade, from sons of dukes, ministers, and chief stewards through the jia, yi, bing, and ding clans, above to scattered cavalry and secretarial posts and below to censor and senior adjutant—all regulations are clear and the text suffers no omission.
idiomatic: By stipend and privilege, from sons of grandees down through the jia–ding grades, from scattered cavalry and secretaries to censors and senior adjutants—every rule was explicit and intact.

literal: From this time persons not sons of the three highest offices have been released from the sack as regular aides in the public offices;
idiomatic: Since then men not of the top three lineages have taken first office as regular aides in government bureaus;

literal: lands not of the jia and yi classes yet attain chief steward and traveling aides.
idiomatic: families below jia–yi rank have reached chief steward and traveling aides.

literal: From this downward there have also been many violations.
idiomatic: Below that level violations multiplied.

literal: Moreover, military adjutant is a specialized post, not an entry office—now men must leave the sack to hold it;
idiomatic: Military adjutant is a specialist post, not an entry rank—yet entrants now hold it at first appointment;

literal: secretarial posts were originally entry offices, yet now men are transferred up to them.
idiomatic: secretary was a starter office, yet men are promoted into it.

literal: These all look up and lose the former standard, violating the bright command.
idiomatic: Each case abandons the old standard and breaches the clear decree.

literal: This is not what is called taking the distant model as law and obeying the completed rule.
idiomatic: That is not "following the ancestral pattern and holding to settled rule."

literal: Though this is the fault of official personnel, followed for a long time, yet pushing its spread, there is also a cause.
idiomatic: Though officials are to blame and the abuse is old, its spread also has a cause.

literal: What is it?
idiomatic: What cause?

literal: To trust one man's clarity against the breadth of the nine currents must make him comprehend clans and discriminate human relations—talent and knowledge are limited and it is inherently hard to examine all.
idiomatic: One man's judgment cannot survey the nine streams of talent, weigh every clan, and judge every bond—capacity is finite and full review impossible.

literal: Therefore the state set the post of rectifier of the center in each province to clarify gates and pedigrees, appraise high and low, one measure for the four seas, solely holding the balance stone—the charge is truly not light.
idiomatic: Hence each province had a rectifier to fix pedigree and rank, one standard for the realm, sole holder of the scales—a weighty charge.

literal: Thus from establishing the rectifier down to the Taihe era, none failed to set high the man and exhaust this selection.
idiomatic: From the rectifier's founding through Taihe, appointees were always eminent and the choice meticulous.

literal: All had to be men whose name and rank outweighed their village and state and whose talent and virtue satisfied public gaze—only then could they judge and cut in the provinces and commanderies and examine persons.
idiomatic: Only when name outweighed the district and talent satisfied all eyes could they grade provinces and weigh candidates.

literal: Those now appointed are mostly not such men; I beg a clear edict and regulation so that in choosing official talent all fully follow the former intent, not letting ability and inability cross positions or violate talent and change duties.
idiomatic: Today's appointees rarely qualify; I beg an edict that selection follow the original rule so merit and post never mismatch.

literal: And abolish the rectifier, wholly following the former track.
idiomatic: Abolish the rectifier and return wholly to the old course.

literal: Then the clear source will have return and the flowing order will be truly solemn.
idiomatic: Then the clear spring will have its channel and ranks will run true.

literal: The Empress Dowager edicted that the memorial be followed and implemented, yet in the end it could not be used.
idiomatic: The Empress Dowager ordered the memorial enacted, but it was never carried out.

literal: What Tongdian records of Northern Wei edicts and memorials generally comes from the Book of Wei; as the two memorials of Gao You and Han Xianzong quoted above both appear in their basic biographies, the Yuan Yi memorial quoted above must also come from the original text of this biography in the Book of Wei.
idiomatic: Tongdian's Northern Wei edicts and memorials usually copy the Book of Wei; since Gao You's and Han Xianzong's papers above appear in their lives, Yuan Yi's table must be the Wei's original here.

literal: The Northern History often deletes edicts and memorials without recording them, or abbreviates them.
idiomatic: Northern History often drops or shortens edicts and memorials.

literal: This memorial may have been omitted from recording, but the affair should still have been noted.
idiomatic: This memorial may have been cut, but the event should have been noted.

literal: Now this biography shows nothing of it; it is suspected that below "five benefits, luck" and so on what fell away is not only the latter part of the memorial on favoring the heavy and pitying the humble, but also Yuan Yi's memorial on selection affairs.
idiomatic: The life is silent on it; likely the lacuna after "five benefits, luck" swallowed not only the end of the remonstrance on favoring the lowly but Yuan Yi's entire memorial on appointments.

literal: A partisan of Cha, direct-access gentleman Song Wei, pleased Cha's intent. Various editions and Northern History juan 19 read "Song Wei" as "Zong Zhun'ai"; Comprehensive Records juan 84b reads "Song Zhun."
idiomatic: Cha's factioner, direct-access gentleman Song Wei, did Cha's bidding. Editions and Northern History 19 have "Zong Zhun'ai" for "Song Wei"; Comprehensive Records 84b has "Song Zhun."

literal: Commentary: In juan 16, appended biography of Yuan Li, Prince of Jingzhao, biography of Yuan Cha, it states: "Cha then had direct-access gentleman Song Wei report to the Director of Dyeworks, Commandant Han Wenshu, plotting rebellion to install Yi."
idiomatic: Note: Yuan Cha's appended life (juan 16, Prince of Jingzhao Li) says Cha had Song Wei accuse Han Wenshu, director of dyeworks, of plotting to set Yi on the throne.

literal: Juan 60, appended biography of Han Lin'ao, biography of his son Xi—Xi and others submitted a memorial vindicating Yuan Yi also says "the boy Song Wei" and so on.
idiomatic: Han Lin'ao's line (juan 60), son Xi's memorial clearing Yuan Yi, likewise calls him "the boy Song Wei."

literal: Song Wei is appended in juan 63, biography of Song Bian; the biography also records this affair.
idiomatic: Song Wei appears under Song Bian (juan 63), which records the same incident.

literal: Here "Zong Zhun" is clearly an error for "Song Wei"; what Zheng Qiao saw in the Northern History biography still had "Song" not yet corrupted to "Zong."
idiomatic: "Zong Zhun" is plainly "Song Wei"; Zheng Qiao's Northern History still read Song before the graph corrupted to Zong.

literal: Now corrected.
idiomatic: Emended accordingly.

literal: The character "ai" is perhaps a superfluous addition, or an error for "yuan"; now deleted.
idiomatic: "Ai" is likely intrusive or a miswrite of yuan—removed.

literal: Those who had their faces split for him numbered several hundred persons. Palace Edition textual notes state: "Split face is an error for flay face."
idiomatic: "Several hundred had their faces split for him": Palace Edition textual notes read split face (pi mian) as flay face (li mian).

literal: Commentary: Comprehensive Records correctly reads "flay face."
idiomatic: Comprehensive Records has the correct "flay face."

literal: Yue set up a great mortar-pestle at the province gate. Qian's Textual Notes juan 38 state: "This is an affair from when Yue was military governor of Xuzhou; above this there is also missing text."
idiomatic: "Yue placed a great pestle at the province gate": Qian's Textual Notes (juan 38) say this belongs to his Xuzhou command—text is missing above.

literal: Commentary: Juan 9, Annals of Emperor Suzong, twelfth month of the fourth year of Zhengguang, states: "The Grand Mentor, Prince of Runan Yue, was made Grand Tutor and governor of Xuzhou."
idiomatic: Suzong annals (juan 9), Zhengguang 4 month 12: "Grand Mentor, Prince of Runan Yue, became Grand Tutor and Xuzhou governor."

literal: Comprehensive Records juan 184b above this sentence has "transferred to Grand Tutor, sent out as governor of Xuzhou"—probably added from the annals.
idiomatic: Comprehensive Records 184b inserts "made Grand Tutor, sent out as Xuzhou governor" above—likely from the annals.

literal: Yan sent his general Wang Bian to escort and place him on the border. Various editions read "Wang Bian" as "Wang Sengbian."
idiomatic: Yan sent general Wang Bian to deliver him to the border; editions expand the name to Wang Sengbian.

literal: Commentary: Juan 58, biography of Yang Yu, shows the Liang general "Wang Bian"; Liang shu juan 33, biography of Yang Kan, writes "Wang Bian"; yet this book's juan 10, Annals of Emperor Xiaozhuang, also writes "Wang Sengbian."
idiomatic: Yang Yu's life (juan 58) names the Liang general Wang Bian; Liang shu 33 (Yang Kan) has Wang Bian; this book's Xiaozhuang annals (juan 10) read Wang Sengbian.

literal: Wang Bian also appears in juan 9, Annals of Emperor Suzong, first month of the third year of Xiaochang; juan 21b, appended biography of Prince of Pengcheng Xie, biography of Yuan Shao; juan 79, biography of Lu Yu.
idiomatic: Wang Bian also appears in Suzong annals (juan 9, Xiaochang 3 month 1), Yuan Shao's life under Prince Xie of Pengcheng (juan 21b), and Lu Yu (juan 79).

literal: The character "seng" was rashly added by later men; now deleted.
idiomatic: Later scribes spuriously added seng (monk)—removed.

literal: See collation note [4] to juan 10.
idiomatic: See textual note [4] to juan 10.

literal: At the beginning of Emperor Chu's reign he was first appointed Grand Marshal and died. Commentary: Juan 1, Annals of Emperor Chu, twelfth month of the first year of Taichang, clearly records Yuan Yue was killed.
idiomatic: "At Chu's accession he was made Grand Marshal and died": Chu annals (juan 1), Taichang 1 month 12, plainly record Yuan Yue was killed.

literal: Northern History juan 19 also says Yue and the Former Deposed Emperor
idiomatic: Northern History 19 likewise says Yue and the Former Deposed Emperor

literal: 〈Prince of Guangling Gong〉
idiomatic: (Prince of Guangling, Gong)

literal: were both by Emperor Xiaowu
idiomatic: were both killed by Emperor Xiaowu

literal: 〈that is, Emperor Chu〉
idiomatic: (i.e., Emperor Chu)

literal: "harmed before and after"—the original is not in error.
idiomatic: "slain in succession"—the received text is correct.

literal: The latter half of this biography does not come from the Northern History, yet writes only "died," as if a peaceful end—deletion is inappropriate.
idiomatic: The life's latter half is not from Northern History, yet says only "died" as though he died in bed—an ill-chosen cut.
